We've also incorporated nulls and functional dependencies into the context of data integration, developing a strategy to manage inconsistencies and missing values in combined data. Lastly, we've included an exhaustive list of open problems in the area of inconsistent tables with nulls and functional dependencies. The study falls under the category of inconsistency management challenges in relational tables. The main research topics related to this study include constraint relaxation, data cleaning, and data integration. Recently, estimating a 6D object pose using Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) has gained significant interest. Literature can be broadly categorized into two main areas based on whether intermediate cues are employed: direct methods and two-stage pipelines. In the latter category, CNN regresses intermediate cues such as object coordinates or virtual control points instead of pose parameters in the initial stage. Object pose is then resolved through clustering of projection points or correspondence of virtual control points with image features. This study builds upon the foundation of an earlier work, DeepHMap, and presents an enhanced framework, named DeepHMap++. In DeepHMap++, two CNNs generate virtual control points and project the object onto an imaginary canvas with specified thickness. Both networks share weights, with the second network producing a quality map that measures the correspondence between projected points and image features. Quality scores are subsequently employed to perform clustering of projection points, leading to a reduced set of distinct points. A global optimizer then finds the best pose match among these points. Experimental results show that DeepHMap++ excels in difficult scenarios with low-resolution images and performs pose estimation for novel views efficiently. Moreover, this framework facilitates derivative applications such as object manipulation and image retrieval. Evaluations have been conducted and presented in the paper, demonstrating the capabilities of the proposed framework. The code has been made publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/lingyu-92/DeepHMap++.

Our new method calculates a variation of eigenvector centrality for multi-layered networks that incorporate node importance across different layers. In these networks, defined by separate interconnected graphs without connections between different layers, the value of a node's centrality is determined by the sum of the values of the connected nodes within each specific layer, similar to traditional eigenvector centrality calculations. Unlike standard approaches, our approach takes into account the relationships between different network layers and their respective impact on the centrality values. Unlike current multi-layer eigenvector centrality frameworks that account for inter-layer connections, our approach uses a separate set of equations that can be solved using a hybrid algorithm. This algorithm first determines the degree of node connectivity within each layer and then uses this information to calculate the centrality values. We validate our method by analyzing a variety of networks including simple single-layer networks, bridge networks, and more complex multi-layer networks featuring both overlapping and isolated components. Our results show that the distribution of centrality values reflects the distribution of node degrees within each layer, and that the network's connectivity structure is accurately captured through the Salnikov vector. Furthermore, we find that the approach is robust and sensitive to network topological changes, and that the resolution can be influenced by adjusting the tolerance parameter. Our method has potential applications in fields such as biology, finance, and security, among others. We conclude by outlining potential future developments and our approach's relationship to existing multi-layer eigenvector centrality theories. Our code is available online.

This surface seal regime, found between low and high-speed impact velocities, features a distinctive "splash dome" formation. Empirical rules describing when the splash dome closes ("pinch-off time") generally hold for both slow-moving and fast-moving spheres, yet require further refinement, especially in the middle speed range. Our key findings include a more precise pinch-off time prediction model for spheres moving at intermediate speeds, along with a detailed analysis of how spheres behave in that speed range. Our results show that increased violence in impact collisions, rather than increased seal time, is the primary factor influencing pinch-off time in that middle speed range. Our research also reveals two distinct surface seal behaviors in that speed range, dependent on violent versus non-violent impact collisions. Our most violent sphere scenario matches previous "splash dome" closure time predictions, while our non-violent sphere scenario reflects the role of elastic sphere deformation in that middle speed range. Our data and predictions highlight surface seal and pinch-off time interactions with elastic deformation, hydrodynamic forces, and sphere velocity in that middle speed range. A burgeoning field in quantum physics, known as quantum dissensive flux flow, is characterized by extremely large amplitude oscillations between a highly populated steady state and a vacuum state, primarily observed in cavity quantum electrodynamics systems. This research involves coupling a quantum system to a cavity and measuring the fluctuations in a output field, which in previous cases has only demonstrated significant amplitude oscillations in a transverse Zeeman subspaces facilitated by a strong external magnetic field. However, our discovery demonstrates that incredibly large amplitude oscillations between a dark exciton state and a vacuum state can be achieved without utilizing an external magnetic field, instead relying on a dark state that is immune to magnetic field fluctuations. When representing this dark state with a combination of Hamiltonian parameters, it exhibits remarkable stability, thereby enabling the reliable production of coherent state fluctuations in a range of conditions. This has been demonstrated through numerical analysis, which shows that the quantum system can maintain its dark state characteristics even when it transitions between different parameter regimes, even including situations with direct interactions between qubits. Consequently, this discovery offers a straightforward and reliable way to generate highly amplified fluctuations in the output field just by adjusting the detuning of one qubit, which has been validated through experimental data. This finding holds significant value for theoretical quantum physics, particularly in cavity quantum electrodynamics, as it enables access to a range of conditions, from a free particle regime to a regime with direct qubit-qubit interactions, via the adjustment of detuning. Furthermore, this research has been conducted on a system consisting of superconducting circuit quantum electrodynamics, which offers vast possibilities for transferring this discovery to other systems, such as semiconductor quantum dot systems, by simply exchanging the qubit detector. This has been achieved through numerical analysis, which shows that all that is required is a change in the system's Hamiltonian, thereby ensuring that this breakthrough is applicable to a broad range of quantum systems. This discovery has been experimentally verified through the measurement of fluctuation amplitude, which shows that it is possible to generate coherent state fluctuations in a range of conditions, even with direct qubit-qubit interactions, via the adjustment of detuning. Our investigation focuses on a 2D electronic lattice from a non-symmorphic wallpaper group, which has been rarely explored. We construct a model representing a honeycomb-lattice surface, with two types of sublattices (A and B) that are shifted relative to each other by half-unit cells in two perpendicular directions. Our analysis reveals the presence of Dirac points at various locations within the first Brillouin zone, depending on the relative phase difference between the two sublattices. By modulating the on-site potential between the A and B sublattices, we can move the position of these Dirac points, creating various shapes, including lines, circles, and squares, around the first Brillouin zone. Our study also reveals possible petal-like and square shapes formed by the connection of Dirac points with each other and the boundary of the Brillouin zone. These predicted results could be realized in a recent experimental setup that incorporates a silicon carbide surface treated with a boron nitride overlay, and are characterized by both theoretical calculations and tight-binding models, offering insights into the interplay between local perturbations and the overall shape of the Dirac shapes along the electron dispersion paths. Next, we propose an experimental approach to visualize the shift of Dirac points by using near-field microscopy to measure the local optical response of the lattice, which reflects the sublattice phase difference. Finally, our findings in a two-dimensional context are compared to similar research conducted in a one-dimensional setting, and we provide a suitable tight-binding model that includes both nearest-neighbor hoppings along the x and y directions, as well as local perturbations in the y direction. This model predicts the occurrence of two types of Dirac points with different orientations along the electron dispersion paths, and the possible shapes that the Dirac points can take on, ranging from lines to squares, and the effect of the local perturbations on the electron spectrum. Next, we discuss a possible experimental approach that could realize this model, and measure the local perturbations and the shape of the Dirac points along the electron dispersion paths. Lastly, we conclude by outlining potential future research avenues, such as investigating flat bands, magnetic ordering, and artificial gauge fields, which could provide additional insights into this fascinating and highly tunable Dirac points system. Quantum states of light play a key role in the development of quantum communication systems. The issue of artifical noise hindering qubit measurement needs to be addressed. The quantum-optical catalysis effect provides a solution to this problem by generating a superposed state from an initial coherent state, followed by a single-photon annihilation operation. This process results in a coherent state embedded in a photon number noise system. However, when a single-photon detection occurs, the state collapses to a noise-free state. The question remains of how to generate the specific state $\cos^2(\theta)|\beta\rangle+\sin^2(\theta)|-\beta\rangle$, which represents a coherent phase. By employing quantum-optical catalysis with a single-photon storage device, we develop an artificial noise-free coherent phase generation system. The condition under which this system produces the desired state is defined. Additionally, the issue of system loss is addressed by analyzing the effect of storage device loss on the state preparation, and proposing a recovery protocol. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this system allows for the generation of a universal quantum cluster state. The approach presented here offers a novel solution for creating artificial coherent phases from single-photon stored light, and the related state preparation procedure is robust against storage device loss. The issue of storage device loss can be resolved by performing a conditional measurement, which restores the original state and allows for the use of leftover photons in subsequent quantum operations. In General Relativity using the Newman-Penrose formalism, the use of bivectors plays a key role in identifying the precise nature of a solution to the Einstein field equations. This review focuses on the fundamental principles of bivectors and their applications within the Newman-Penrose formalism, specifically by analyzing the key components of the Weyl tensor in complex geometry. We examine the concept of the Weyl curvature index, initially introduced by Harrison, which serves as a measure of the complexibility of a spacetime's conformal structure. This index can be determined based on the eigenvalues of a specific complex matrix derived from the Weyl tensor's components in the Newman-Penrose formalism. We then delve into the physical interpretations of the Weyl curvature index in both electromagnetic and gravitational contexts. In the case of electromagnetism, the index represents the number of electromagnetic waves present in a spacetime, while in General Relativity, it is associated with the memory effect caused by massive gravitational waves. We also discuss the algebraic classification of the Weyl tensor and the relationship between the Weyl curvature index and this classification. Furthermore, we explore the possible values the Weyl curvature index can take, including its behavior under null congruences and its relationship with the scalar curvature invariants. We also examine the connection between the Weyl curvature index and the complex geometry of a spacetime, specifically in the context of Allen-Harrison's theorem, and in cases where the spacetime's conformal structure is complex, as determined by the index's value. We also discuss the implications of the Weyl curvature index for the algebraic components of the Einstein tensor and the matter tensor in General Relativity. We then review the mathematical frameworks for the Newman-Penrose formalism, complex geometry, and the Weyl curvature index in both electromagnetic and gravitational contexts. We also examine the physical and mathematical interpretations of the Weyl curvature index, specifically in the context of Allen-Harrison's theorem, complex geometry, and the index's relationship with the scalar curvature invariants. We also discuss the possible future directions for researching the Newman-Penrose formalism, complex geometry, and the Weyl curvature index in General Relativity. Identifying tumors in the esophagus from CT scans can be very difficult for humans or computer systems due to low contrast, the varying shape of the esophagus, and the presence of external objects such as feeding tubes. To compensate for these difficulties, doctors often rely on supplementary information from other imaging techniques, medical histories, and endoscopic findings. Acquiring and combining these sources of information is time-consuming and sometimes produces inconclusive results. In this study, we investigate the potential for a quicker and more efficient approach using alone CT scans for the accurate segmentation of esophageal tumors. To this end, we present a novel deep learning-based method called Dense Focus Unet (DFU) and demonstrate its high performance when compared to traditional techniques and other state-of-the-art models on a publicly available dataset. Moreover, we show that this method's simplicity allows for a significant decrease in processing time while maintaining a high level of accuracy. The code for this research has been made available at https://github.com/ghassabzadeh/DFUUnet. The resulting model has also been deployed as a tool for real-time clinical applications. The findings of this research have been published in the journal Medical Physics [1]. The model has been further improved and a version called DDAUnet has been presented at the IEEE-ISBI conference and the code for this model can be found at https://github.com/ghassabzadeh/DDAUnet. The DDAUnet model has also been deployed as a part of a workflow for real-time clinical applications available at https://github.com/ghassabzadeh/EsophagusSegmentation. The findings of this research have been published in the journal IEEE Transactions on Medical Imaging [2]. The code for the DDAUnet model has been selected for inclusion in the MICCAI 2022 Challenge on Multiple Organ Segmentation from Abdominal CT [3]. Code-mixed languages encompass the diverse ways different languages are combined in texts, varying from mixed syntax to embedded languages within sentences. This categorization is particularly prevalent among social media content, where it represents the dominant form of communication. Despite this frequency, code-mixed texts present significant challenges for NLP techniques due to lacking standardization, which further standardization efforts strive to address. Our work focuses on examining the complex issues NLP engineers encounter when dealing with code-mixed data, from fundamental theoretical problems to practical applications in various tasks. We also explore key factors that influence the development of NLP models for combined languages, such as dataset characteristics, model design, and quality assessment methods. By delving into these aspects, we aim to contribute to further research and provide a foundation for future inquiries in this emerging field. The paper is targeted towards the audience of the 4th Workshop on Human Computation and Crowdsourcing, given the connection between crowdsourced efforts and code-mixed language data. However, the topics we cover are relevant to a broader NLP audience interested in NLP for multilingual populations. We hope this work to also contribute to the crowd-sourcing and multi-lingual NLP communities by exploring approaches to evaluate the effectiveness of various NLP techniques for combined languages. Given the diverse formats code-mixed languages can take and the variety of evaluation metrics used, we propose a framework for evaluating these metrics in relation to different code-mixed categorizations. Quantifying the quality of automatic image descriptions is crucial, and one widely used method for evaluation is by comparing them with human-generated descriptions. Although this approach seems straightforward, it can lead to false assumptions about the effectiveness of existing description generation techniques. By analyzing existing datasets that comprise human-described images along with their corresponding scores in a benchmark assessment, we demonstrate how a particular average benchmark score can be reached by automatic descriptions without surpassing the lowest human- scored description for that image. Furthermore, we highlight instances where the diversity of human descriptions incorporates automatic descriptions with significantly lower scores, indicating room for improvement in existing techniques. By taking a more nuanced view of human-described data and benchmark assessments, our study provides a more precise understanding of the capabilities and limitations of automatic image description generation. We also propose a novel metric, the worst score, to provide a more comprehensive evaluation of these techniques. This metric can be employed in conjunction with other evaluation methods to provide a more comprehensive analysis of description generation models. We support this idea with code available online. Our study revolves around the existing CCSD dataset but offers actionable advice applicable to other human-described image description datasets. Our novel worst score metric can be effectively utilized in various evaluation settings, including during the development phase of models, using a batch of human descriptions, as well as in leading benchmark evaluation platforms, by incorporating the worst score of human descriptions for each image. This approach provides an intuitive and straightforward method for evaluating the worst description for each image, which can be achieved by ranking all human descriptions associated with an image and determining the score of the least favorable description. Our study highlights the importance of qualifying the benchmark data used for evaluation, which is crucial for avoiding misleading conclusions about the effectiveness of description generation techniques. We demonstrate this necessity by presenting a specific average benchmark score that can be reached by automatic descriptions without them exceeding the lowest human-scored description for that image. Our findings also offer a more nuanced understanding of the diversity of human descriptions, which is essential for evaluating description generation techniques. We conclude by outlining future research directions, including but not limited to, investigating the relationship between the diversity of human descriptions and the quality of description generation techniques, as well as developing methods for evaluating the diversity of human descriptions. Tantalum oxide compounds, with the formula Ta$_2$O$_5$, are distinguished by unique properties including high dielectric values and minimal reflectivity. To further understand and identify these materials, theoretical studies have been conducted using first-principles calculations and Monte Carlo simulations to explore Ta$_2$O$_5$'s possible lattice structures at both room temperature and theoretically optimal conditions. When considering different configurations of oxygen octahedra arrangements, researchers found that Ta$_2$O$_5$ has a complex nature, allowing multiple valid ground state interpretations. This indication of structural polymorphism could be responsible for the material's reflective or dielectric behavior, though more experimental analysis is required to confirm this hypothesis. This theoretical work also presents feasible routes to synthesize both rock-salt and corundum-tantalum Ta$_2$O$_5$ structures, ending with a discussion on potential applications and areas for future research.

The Big Geographic Shift, a demographic change where younger people moved from rural to urban areas, has been hypothesized to contribute to the spread of misinformation. To examine this hypothesis, we analyzed posts containing false information on Reddit forums covering the Reddit platform's entire geographical scope. By leveraging user-generated location tags and combining them with false information detection utilizing multiple fact-checking sources, we identified and classified posts as containing misinformation in one of four categories: health, political, economic/environmental, or other. A comparative study of these categories across subreddits corresponding to specific US regions revealed variations in misinformation circulation. Furthermore, we utilized statistical modeling to assess the Big Geographic Shift's impact on misinformation circulation, factoring in elements like demographic changes, urbanization, and COVID-19-related information expansion. Our findings showed that the Big Geographic Shift accelerated the circulation of economic/health misinformation in urban areas, and that this shift's effect on misinformation circulation differed by topic than in studies citing online platforms' reliance on news sources as contributing factors. Consequently, our research supports the hypothesis that the Big Geographic Shift contributed to the spread of economic/health misinformation, and highlights the significance of considering the social and geographical contexts in which misinformation circulates. Our study's facts-based methodology can be applied to other false information research cases. Our discovery of differing misinformation circulation patterns across urban and rural areas also has implications for the distribution of true information, as we observed opposing effects on the circulation of political/economic misinformation. Our study suggests that researchers should analyze the Big Geographic Shift's impact on misinformation circulation, and explores the shift's potential influence on the consolidation of media industries and demographic change. Our findings on the contexts in which misinformation circulates can be expanded to other false information cases, as we developed a statistical model based on fact-checked information sources. Our research on the Big Geographic Shift and its influence on misinformation circulation can be applied to other topics, such as the circulation of true information, or the distribution of other phenomena affected by demographic change, urbanization, or COVID-19. Humans employ spoken language to efficiently convey complex tasks to robots, but the effectiveness of this approach depends on a clear understanding of how speech conveys practical task information. While previous research primarily focuses on text-based robot programming, our study explores the connection between spoken language and action by analyzing demonstrations given to robots by human instructors through speech and physical motion. We investigated four key aspects of demonstration speech: sequence structure, physical action references, object references, and instruction commands. Our analysis revealed that demonstration speech follows a linear sequence reflecting the physical and temporal aspects of tasks, with the majority of spoken content dedicated to describing a task's components rather than its overall structure. We found that humans typically use nominal phrases to refer to objects and infinite verb phrases to refer to actions, and that demonstration speech often incorporates repetitions and elaborations to ensure successful task comprehension. By decomposing demonstration speech into its fundamental components, our study provides a clear and concrete understanding of spoken language's structural and syntactic characteristics that underlie its ability to convey actionable task information. We also present a validated analysis tool that can extract actionable information from demonstration speech, confirming that this tool's predictions align with human assessments of the same speech. Our research has significant implications for the development of speech-based robot programming systems and offers a foundation for further investigation into demonstration speech's functional elements, such as its relationship to task variability and the effectiveness of instruction commands. We make our research publicly available through the following GitHub link: https://github.com/AIResearchLab/SpeechActionDecomposer.

Cross-domain recommendation has been gaining significant attention for addressing the pervasive issue of data sparsity in recommender systems. Single-target and dual-target scenarios are prevalent, but multi-sparse-domain cooperative recommendation, which is largely unexplored, can provide even more comprehensive suggestions by considering multiple domains with varying levels of sparsity. Existing methods often concentrate on establishing connections based on user behavior, without sufficiently addressing the diversity of sparsity domains. To tackle this challenge, we introduce a Multi-Sparse-Domain Cooperative Recommendation framework, MSDCRF, which leverages enhanced comprehensive aspect preference learning to effectively manage user preference homogeneity and diversity of sparsity across domains. User behavior is represented as a complex dynamic network to capture dynamic preferences and structural variability. With consideration given to domain-specific preference and diversity, MSDCRF employs a multi-objective optimization approach to enhance aspect-based preference and a comprehensive learning method to ensure seamless adaptation to dynamic preferences. Experimental evaluations on real-world datasets demonstrate the superiority of MSDCRF in handling multi-sparse-domain data with varied levels of sparsity and complexity. The system's scalability and flexibility are also highlighted with low computational overhead and easy adaptation to domain dynamics. The implementation is further illustrated with an e-commerce case study. The code for MSDCRF has been publicly released to facilitate future research and real-world applications. The system achieves notable performance boosts over baseline methods in multiple evaluation metrics. The analysis of the dataset sparsity domains reveals distinct patterns of sparsity and complexity among real-world datasets. The results highlight the diversity of sparsity domains and their impact on recommendation performance. The analysis suggests that a uniform distribution of sparsity domains may lead to performance degradation due to overwhelming noise from medium- and highly-sparse domains. This extension is made possible by assigning a specific conic structure to each variable in the equation, such as the ratio structure, the reciprocal structure, and the logarithmic structure, which can be viewed as a natural generalization of the traditional conic structures like the absolute value structure, the ratio structure, and the logarithmic structure. This document outlines the fundamentals of Hypatia Julia, a Julia implementation of the primal-dual interior-point method for solving conic equations, and provides a straightforward example of solving a nonlinear conic equation using the method. Additionally, Hypatia Julia is compared to the Julia implementation of the limited-memory quasi-Newton method for solving nonlinear optimization problems. In a second example, Hypatia Julia is applied to the difficulty-to-interpret factor model, a financial risk management model, and to the George model, a model for estimating credit risk. Both of these models involve complex conic equations and have previously been solved using other, more cumbersome methods. The escalating quantity of MRI data necessitates automated quality assessment to ensure reliable and efficient analysis, especially for extensive research projects. Several approaches have been explored to develop scalable and dependable quality assurance processes, including machine learning-based methods that utilize limited training data. This study's objective is to investigate the feasibility of a MRI data quality assessment model that can generalize across multiple factors, such as different MRI modalities, data collection methods, and specific research study characteristics, which can pose a challenge due to modality-specific anomalies and study-dependent population coverage. We developed a multi-factorial generalization quality assessment model using MRI data from two different modalities, collected over a period of seven years, with varying data collection processes. Our evaluation shows that this model achieves a 93% accuracy in classifying data as pass or fail, and significantly outperforms alternative methods in multiple aspects. Our approach demonstrates a promising way to develop MRI data quality assessment models that can be adapted for widespread applications. To understand how private electric vehicles influence the resilience of distribution networks, we developed a decision-making framework for optimal charging and driving paths utilizing agent optimization techniques. This framework considers the non-cooperative behavior of EV owners and accounts for the physical constraints of the grid and transportation systems. We utilized a set-based optimization method to introduce valid inequalities that enhance solution solutions, and a sub-optimality threshold to limit the depth of our search for optimal solutions. Additionally, we implemented a numerical procedure to calculate the distribution network's risk of collapse due to extreme events. Our research was conducted using a small-scale transportation and energy network, and we analyzed the effects of different EV penetration levels, transportation networks, and grid infrastructure on the network's resilience. Our findings indicate that during normal conditions, the distribution network can generally operate within its limits, but may still experience limitations due to heavy EV usage. However, during extreme events, the network's vulnerability to collapse is significantly influenced by the size of the transportation network, but not the level of grid infrastructure. We also discovered that the distribution network's limits are often breached as a result of EV owner's self-interested behavior, which can have negative implications for grid maintenance and infrastructure planning. We recommend adopting policies that prioritize the maintenance of transportation networks and provide incentives for EV owners to operate within the network's capacity, which can help mitigate these issues and promote more sustainable transportation. We believe our research can be applied to other settings beyond distribution networks and electric vehicles, and provides a general framework for evaluating the resilience of interconnected systems affected by multiple stressors. We have made our code available online for replication purposes. We propose a new metric, the distribution network's loading threshold, which can be used to guide management decisions and mitigate the risk of network collapse. We also outline a pathway for future research, including a study on the dynamics of the transportation network and a examination of the impact of grid infrastructure on network resilience. In this research, a novel framework for creating complex meetings with multiple agents is introduced by incorporating a motivational drive-based system. This framework provides multiple agents with distinct roles, task-specific motivations, and individual decision-making capabilities to interact and collaborate within a meeting session. As a result of their interactions, the agents develop a cohesive plan of action that meets the session's objectives. A notable feature of this system is that it allows for multiple possible outcomes from a single meeting session, resulting from the diverse decision-making processes of individual agents. To validate this research, experimental studies were conducted to examine the variety of solutions generated and their fit to the designed framework. These experiments revealed that in many cases, the diversity of solutions exceeds the desired level, indicating room for improvement. To address this limitation, additional experiments were conducted to examine the effectiveness of two approaches aimed at reducing solution diversity and enhancing adaptation within the meeting session. The results of these experiments showed that both proposed solutions are effective in their own right and can be combined to create an integrated system that in turn can be further customized to suit specific needs. The code for this research is publicly available on GitHub at the specified URL. The underlying theory of the drive-based motivation system has broad applications in various contexts that demand individual adaptation and complex decision-making, as demonstrated in the accompanying paper titled: The Drive-Based Motivation System: Theory, Algorithm, and Code.

This paper examines the structural, electronic, and magnetic characteristics of GdSn3, CmSn3, and the series GdxCm1-xSn3 ($x = 0.25$, $0.5$, and $0.75$) using a full-potential linearized augmented plane wave method within the generalized gradient approximation+U. We studied the fundamental properties of bulk GdSn3, CmSn3, and GdxCm1-xSn3 materials crystallizing in the AuCu3 structure. Our results match previous experimental and theoretical data on the GdSn3 compound and indicate that CmSn3 and GdSn3 both adopt a type-A anti-ferromagnetic configuration and display metallic behavior. Notably, the magnetic moment diminishes with rising Cm content in the GdxCm1-xSn3 series, and these materials share some key characteristics, rendering them promising for spintronic technology applications. Additionally, we explored the effects of external stress and inter-atomic coupling on the electronic and magnetic properties of the materials. Lastly, we suggest possible synthesis approaches for these materials.

The quest for identifying patterns in the masses of fundamental particles is an intriguing one.  The study describes predicted extensions to the standard model of particle physics, which include novel baryons and mesons that could be discovered in high-energy particle experiments.  A range of theories, such as expanded symmetries of the standard model, suggests that additional fundamental particles may possess properties similar to those of quarks and leptons.  By applying these expanded symmetries to a system of combined quark and lepton pairs, researchers have theoretically calculated the masses of possible baryons and mesons that could be found in high-energy particle collisions.  The study indicates that experiments at the Large Hadron Collider, a powerful particle accelerator based on the European Organization for Nuclear Research (CERN) facility in Switzerland, have the capability to detect specific types of baryons and mesons with the equivalent of a small amount of data from its current operation level.  As the collider produces more data, researchers expect a broader understanding of particle dynamics and possibly even the identification of new forces of nature.  The study also highlights the potential for future particle accelerators, such as a powerful machine based on the Fermilab facility in the United States, to discover a vast array of additional baryons and mesons that could reveal hidden patterns in the masses of fundamental particles.  The predicted discovery of these particles in experiments could mark a significant breakthrough in the study of physics and earn the 2017 Breakthrough Prize in Physics. The Pantheon SN Ia dataset can be combined with weak lensing observations to constrain the Hubble constant and model the distribution of mass within the universe. By applying a new method to analyze the pantheon data, researchers found that the average mass distortion field within the universe is $\sim 1.1$ times more dense than previously estimated, using a model that incorporates both gravitational lensing and light bending. As a result, the predicted value for the average mass density within the universe is $\sim 3.07 \times 10^{13} \, h^2 \, \Omega_c \, h^2$, which is $\sim 50\%$ higher than previously calculated. Additionally, the analysis revealed that the standard model of the universe holds true, with the exception of a discrepancy of at least an order of magnitude in the predicted level of lensing effects on SN Ia distances. Furthermore, the analysis highlights the significant impact that future weak lensing observations of deep SN Ia surveys will have on reducing this uncertainty and the inherent ambiguity in the standard model of the universe. As such, combining SN Ia data with weak lensing observations is now a critical component in understanding the universe, and future surveys will play a key role in achieving this goal. Research on silicon material for photonic communications has primarily focused on wafer methods, with little exploration of bulk silicon, except when it contains oxygen-related defects.  This study discovers that silicon containing 32 ppm of oxygen can develop T nodes through high temperature processing, and finds that T nodes share the same formation condition as interface states, which control the silicon's 60-degree periodic rotation.  By developing a silicon multi-state T-node model, researchers demonstrate the impact of T nodes on silicon's photonic properties and identify suitable conditions for reducing silicon's rotation periods to 30 degrees.  This leads to a 20% increase in silicon's optical bandwidth and allows for the development of 32 ppm silicon-based photonic frequency rotation nodes with precise 60-degree and 30-degree rotation periods.  This breakthrough also enables researchers to form complex silicon T-node lattices and confirms that T nodes can be effectively reduced or expanded to any desired rotation period, simply by adjusting the silicon's oxygen content during processing.  This development paves the way for silicon-based photonic communications systems that use frequency rotation nodes, and demonstrates a flexible and adjustable method for controlling silicon's T-node geometry. For our task that considers context, a suitable object detector is needed.
Different object detectors exploit scene context for recognition in varying ways.
This study categorizes object detectors into 3 groups based on context usage:
one that doesn't use context by isolating the input, another that uses partial
context by isolating part of the feature map, and one that uses full context
without isolation.
Our assessment of deep object detectors reveals that most don't clearly follow
these strategies or explicitly state their approach.
Therefore, this study evaluates the default configurations of popular object
detectors to understand the default behavior of their authors.
Our evaluation shows that using a frozen backbone allows for context use,
and choosing a simple backbone doesn't necessarily imply a simple architecture.
Our analysis of object detectors' context behavior could be a starting point
for improving the representation learning of feature extractors. Our assessments
are demonstrated on the MNIST, CIFAR, and STL-10 datasets, which show that
object detectors can be effective without any modification by performing
classification tasks. Our evaluation code is available at the following link: https://github.com/ghrua/context-assessment.

A key challenge in establishing a functional organ allocation market through altruistic donors is identifying an optimal acceptance policy for unmatched organs. This study explores the ideal acceptance strategy for unpaired kidneys in a setting where willing donors trade kidneys for transplants. By formulating the problem as a stochastic dynamic programming problem, we have derived several key results, including: in a continuous time framework with renal exchange, the optimal policy involves accepting any kidney offer; in a discrete time framework, the optimal policy can be complex, however in 2007, Abraham and Roth demonstrated that a simple 'threshold' policy was optimal when considering waitlist length as the key variable. We have also analyzed the financial and waitlist length outcomes resulting from these optimal policies. Furthermore, we have tested these ideal policies on real world data, showcasing their practical utility. The findings presented in this study are relevant to various organ allocation markets, including kidney exchange, liver allocation, and lung allocation, and can be used by healthcare managers to design and evaluate efficient organ allocation protocols. The data used in this study comprises real world kidney exchange data from 2005 to 2019 in the United States. This paper undertakes a comprehensive mathematical examination of the word2vec model, particularly in its implementation with the Skip-gram learning method. We investigate how NLP embeddings, now widely applied, are impacted by the distribution of terms within a given corpus. A mathematical framework is employed to elucidate the implicit structural assumptions of the model, revealing its reliance on Markovian assumptions that provide a clear theoretical understanding of how embeddings are generated and capture the essence of frequentist synonyms. We also develop generative models and conduct explicit analyses of commonly used loss functions. To further illustrate the limitations of these models, we create synthetic corpora with varying levels of complexity, demonstrating the ability (or inability) of word2vec to effectively learn these structures. We also empirically assess the capabilities of these models using a substantial financial news dataset covering 12 years and spanning 42 million articles, relying on the Loughran-McDonald Sentiment Word Lists. Our results show that these models are prone to confusing antonyms as frequentist synonyms and mixing terms with opposing polarities. Notably, our research also uncovers the non-stationarity of financial corpora, revealing time-varying patterns in cosine similarity among polarized words or company names. Our analysis highlights the entangled mixture of semantic and co-occurring word distributions that these models are capturing, posing challenges for their disentanglement. Our work also offers a mathematical basis for the often-observed analogy relationships among company names, providing a path for further exploration. We conclude that, while these models have achieved a high level of performance in many applications, they are not necessarily understanding the concept of polarities as intended by Loughran-McDonald, and that a more nuanced approach is needed to capture the complex structures of natural language. We suggest possible avenues for such an approach, including using Hamiltonian Neural Networks, Hamiltonian Differential Equators, or alternative learning methods that can disentangle the underlying semantics from the co-occurring distributions. Our code is available at https://github.com/ghassab/word2vec-dynamics.

In multiagent systems, an equilibrium is a stable state where agents' actions do not change, reflecting a balance of interests and potential countermeasures. However, the complexity of the underlying system often results in opaque equilibria, making it difficult to understand the underlying dynamics and validate the accuracy of the detected equilibrium. In response to this challenge, our approach enables the detection of an explainable equilibrium in multiagent systems, along with a corresponding policy for each agent that can be trained end-to-end using reinforcement learning principles. To accomplish this, we introduce a new reinforcement learning framework that incorporates a contrastive loss function to produce a visible and coherent policy distribution, resulting in an explainable equilibrium that accurately reflects the true distribution of the system. In our experiments, we demonstrate that this approach outperforms the non-explainable baseline in systems with linear dynamics and show that the approach is applicable to complex systems with nonlinear dynamics, as evidenced by our successful implementation in an intricate multiplayer game requiring strategic action. System and game-specific features can be effectively integrated into the model, and the approach offers cost-effective performance compared to the non-explainable baseline in various scenarios. The code for this research is publicly accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/ChengxiangPan/ExEQ.

The model involves an undirected graph whose edges change at unknown rates based on the number of infections they connect. The main focus is on determining the expected time the epidemic takes to spread to a specific node, with the aim of identifying key characteristics of the spread time compared to the rate at which edges change. The study provides initial results on the epidemic spread time, along with three distinct cases of edge change rates that lead to explicit formulas for the expected time to spread to a particular node. The study also examines how the epidemic spread time changes in response to changes in the rate at which edges change, including rates that result in a changing number of degrees for the node in question. The main findings are then applied to three specialized graph structures: a single-edge graph, a complete graph, and a linear chain graph. The analysis covers not only the outcomes for an epidemic model with preventive rewiring but also provides historical results on models with permanent rewiring for comparison purposes. We introduce a method for conducting comprehensive N-body simulations of various cosmological theories in a rapid and economical manner. This technique enables us to perform an all-around, precise simulation of cosmological dynamics in a matter-dominated era, accounting for the effects of modified gravity. We apply and test this method through simulations of conformally coupled scalar gravity, evaluating the impact of this modification on structure formation and validating our results by comparing them to existing studies. Consequently, these simulations are readily available for incorporating into alternative cosmological scenarios and for using as pseudo-data in future analyses of cosmic microwave background and large-scale structure data. We provide access to a limited set of simulation results, comprising 20 individual simulations of a single simulation run, each with a distinct set of random seed values used in the implementation of the N-body simulation. We also outline a basic framework for conducting such N-body simulations in the context of cosmological theories, including the specifics of our implementation using the RAMSES-Nbody code. Finally, we discuss the key features of conformally coupled scalar gravity and the results of our simulations, covering the expansion history, the evolution of the Hubble constant, the formation of structure, and the characteristics of over 5000 halos. These simulations can be used as a tool for comparing observational predictions of this specific modification of general relativity against those of standard $\Lambda$CDM. We make our simulation data publicly available by contributing it to the Cosmological Large-scale Structure Database. The results of these simulations have been previously studied in a broader analysis of general modified gravity theories, specifically in the work of an associated research paper. The methodology developed here has implications for future studies of general modified gravity theories and provides a framework for evaluating the effects of specific modifications of general relativity."#.

Specifically, we demonstrate that any multiple SLE (with weights derived from the beta random log-gas model) can be viewed as a local boundary behavior of a combined system consisting of a Gaussian free field and multiple Schramm-Loewner evolutions. Furthermore, we establish that these combined systems evolve in a stochastic manner, driven by a process known as the Dyson model. In the context of the beta random log-gas model, this translates to an equivalence between the statistics of the model and the combined system consisting of a Gaussian free field and multiple Schramm-Loewner evolutions. As a result, we obtain precise expressions for the expectation values of geometric variables associated with the random curves, as well as the distribution functions of these variables. In the process, our findings also provide an alternative derivation of the results obtained by script W. Werner and H. A. Nguyen in the specific case of the beta random log-gas model. Additionally, we establish that the combined systems consisting of a Gaussian free field and multiple Schramm-Loewner evolutions are topologically non-trivial, and as such, they exhibit connections to the Riemann surface approach used by D. Choudary, D. Feldheim, and S. Pal, as well as to the combined system consisting of a Gaussian free field and a single Schramm-Loewner evolution on a specific surface with multiple boundary components. This in turn allows us to statistically characterize the behavior of geometric variables associated with random curves on this surface. Lastly, our findings also provide an alternative interpretation of the results obtained by H.A. Nguyen in the specific case of the beta random log-gas model, specifically with regard to the distribution of the length of a single interface within an array of randomly curved interfaces. In this context, our results demonstrate that the probability density function of the length of a single interface is directly equivalent to the probability density function of a specific combined system consisting of a Gaussian free field and a single Schramm-Loewner evolution, and as such, it can be statistically characterized using the parameters of this combined system. As such, our results also provide an answer to the question posed by H.A. Thermodynamics and disorderly motion play a significant role in the functionality and malfunctioning of materials, especially those with low entropy phases. Despite their significance, difficulties in experimental detection have limited our knowledge of these interactions. Until now, understanding of electron-phonon and spin-phonon interactions has been largely static, focusing on the constant stimulation of local vibration and spin fluctuations by electrons. In this study, we reveal the presence of dynamic electron-phonon and spin-phonon interactions resulting from the back and forth motion of electrons and phonons, which generate oscillatory shifts in their interaction rates. These dynamic interactions influence the energy and probability of electron-spin coupling to vibrations, and may lead to notable effects on the formation of solids, their lattice dimensions, and the distribution of their electron spins. Furthermore, we find that the motion of electrons and vibrations harbors intricate interdependent patterns, potentially leading to nonlinear feedback that accelerates the decay of long-lived solid states and contributes to thermal phase transitions. Our findings are applicable to a broad range of materials, from insulating and conducting solids to superconducting and magnetic phases. This research was inspired by experimental observations in molecular conductors, specifically salenetype complexes, but its implications extend to the study of forsterite minerals, polyoxometalates, and other materials influenced by spin-phonon and electron-phonon interactions. Our approach was numerical, based on exact solutions of a simplified model that highlights the fundamental role of momentum thermodynamics and disorderly motion in the function and malfunctioning of materials. Understanding the meaning of conversations relies on grasping the semantics of individual turns and combining them to capture the overall meaning of the dialogue. In this paper, we explore the connection between dialogue semantics and Natural Language Inference (NLI). We introduce a new NLI dataset, called Dialogue NLI (DNILI), which consists of statements about dialogues along with corresponding inference labels. Our findings reveal that NLI models are not necessarily better at predicting statements about dialogues than they are at predicting statements about individual turns, and that both struggle significantly. We also discover that both turn-level and statement-level NLI models struggle to accurately predict labels for certain semantic varieties, including cases where the speaker's opinion changes or remains consistent, or where the addressee's response is or is not an appropriate inference. To enhance the accuracy of NLI predictions in the context of dialogues, we propose a simple yet effective approach that involves training a set of separate BART models on DNILI. Our results show that this approach yields superior performance compared to a variety of baselines, including sequences-to-sequences T5 models. Our proposed method is applicable to both individual turns and dialogue NLI tasks and serves as a suitable alternative for other complicated datasets as well. Our code is available at github.com/salemt/DialogueNLI. For every discussion about this paper, please contact salemt@mit.edu.

We define a distinguished class of valued domains, calling them total domains, such that their local rings possess a specific property - every pair of maximal ideals can be mapped totally by a local ring homomorphism. Total domains are then characterized by their integration theory, specifically through the totality of their valued field. This property is also shown to be equivalent to the integrality domain's having a specific property called strong stability. Within the framework of equicharacteristic extensions, a domain's total nature is found to be stable under extension, although it's not a recursive property. The work presented herein also discusses the connection between total domains and the geometric property of being unramified, a notion we introduce as part of the paper's results. In order to make efficient use of power-consuming CPU frequencies, a new approach is proposed in this research. A GPU-accelerated methodology is developed to determine the optimal CPU frequency schedule, considering various workload characteristics and different power consumption models. The proposed strategy, called HyperDegrade, utilizes machine learning to identify relevant workload features and a binary integer programming model to find the ideal frequency schedule. The results of HyperDegrade demonstrate significant performance improvements in frequency consolidation: on one hand, when using real workload data, the efficiency of CPU frequency schedule reaches 98% on average; on the other hand, in fictitious scenarios simulating real applications, the methodology achieves an average speedup of 12 times and an average energy reduction of 90% in the GPU environment, and an average speedup of 7 times and an average energy reduction of 80% in the bare-metal environment. The researchers also tested HyperDegrade on real systems by deploying the GPU-based methodology on an open-source benchmark platform, and found that in addition to reducing energy consumption, the methodology is capable of discovering hidden bottlenecks in workloads, as well as providing accurate prediction capabilities. The research shows that there is plenty of room for optimizing CPU frequency schedules, and that HyperDegrade opens up new avenues for research in this area. The researchers provide the methodology and benchmark data of HyperDegrade on the website of the IEEE/ACM CCGrid conference. In our study, we demonstrated how both a group that operates permutely on a set and the Cartesian system consisting of which contains subgroups for each element type can be determined from the product of a group that acts on each element type. This process can be achieved via a straightforward algorithm. Additionally, our research reveals that both a permutative group base and the Cartesian system are invariant under any automorphism of the original group. Furthermore, we established that both the group base and the Cartesian system are characteristically simple if and only if the original group is characteristically simple. Both the group base and the Cartesian system are soluble if and only if the original group is soluble. We established that the Fitting subgroup of the original group is tantamount to the group base's derived subgroup, and that both the group base and the Cartesian system are solvable with maximum length 2 if and only if the original group has a solvable chain of length 2. We concluded that both the group base and the Cartesian system are abelian if and only if the original group is abelian. We also proved that the group base's centre is equal to the original group's centre, and that both the group base and the Cartesian system are totally characteristic in the original group. We established that the group base and the Cartesian system are equivalent for finite nilpotent groups, and provided an example to illustrate that this level of congruence does not extend to infinite nilpotent groups. We also investigated under what conditions the group base and the Cartesian system are isomorphic. We concluded by analysing the relationship between the group base and the Cartesian system's subgroups, and examining the group base's and the Cartesian system's composition operators. Lastly, we demonstrated how the group base and the Cartesian system can be applied to a specific category of groups known as parabolic groups.

The ability of advanced gravitational wave detectors to perceive high-frequency signals is hindered by the residual noise in the 40-150 Hz range. To address this limitation, a novel concept called the sloshing Sagnac interferometer has been proposed, which could serve as a monolithic construction for future detectors. However, evaluating the effectiveness of this design is complicated due to its complex noise sources, demanding numerical simulations to assess its performance. In this study, we developed an advanced analysis method that applies a combination of numerical and analytical techniques to investigate the sloshing Sagnac design's noise characteristics. Our findings show that the noise sources associated with the sloshing Sagnac design can be similar to those of the recycled advanced laser interferometric gravitational wave detector. Furthermore, the effectiveness of various noise reduction techniques has been evaluated, and the potential for improving the frequency range of future detectors through optimization of the geometric parameters has been demonstrated. Specifically, our research indicates that the noise associated with the sloshing Sagnac design could be reduced to the level of the recycled advanced detector by constructing the detector from specific materials, such as limestone, and optimizing its geometric parameters, which could then result in the detection of binary neutron star mergers with total mass up to $12.5M_\odot$. The code used in this study has been made available online. The research highlights the promise of the sloshing Sagnac design and the effectiveness of noise reduction techniques, which could also apply to other detector designs. The findings have implications for future detectors, such as Eco and Megana, that incorporate similar constructions. The research has been conducted as part of the Australian gravitational wave research group's activities. The code developed in this study is compatible with the LIGO's Viridian environment. In large-scale MIMO systems, a an access control protocol has been proposed to prevent interconnections between cells' communication areas, ensuring the regions remain non-intersecting. This protocol arranges cells into a hierarchical structure, with smaller cells grouped into larger ones at various tiers. The focus of this research is on analyzing the visibility region dimensions in the second tier of this hierarchy, where each cell's region is non-overlapping with its neighbors. To determine the optimal dimensionality, researchers tested various scale settings and compared the outcomes to a benchmark model, finding that a hierarchy with two tiers offers the best results. Furthermore, this research provides empirical evidence showing that a hierarchy with two tiers, despite reducing capacity, significantly lowers collisions and improves throughput. Moreover, a critical mass phenomenon was observed, where a minimum number of cells is required for improved throughput beyond a certain point, and this research investigates the implications of this phenomenon for the access control protocol. Lastly, a novel algorithm was developed to optimize the hierarchy's structure in response to changes in the system, resulting in a improved throughput throughput of up to 58% through a representative scenario. This research was previously known under the name "Exploiting Non-Intersecting Visibility Regions in XL-MIMO Random Access Protocol".

Neural language models have largely surpassed $N$-gram models due to better performance, but our findings suggest that $n$-gram models still excel in many situations with certain modifications. We discovered that a simplified model, which we call the Basic Gram Model, outperforms current state-of-the-art neural language models in various assessments. Additionally, when combined with neural models, the Basic Gram Model achieves significant improvements in many evaluations, often by 10-20%. We were able to enhance the basic model to the Enhanced Gram Model with the incorporation of embedding techniques and negative sampling, which allowed it to achieve notable results in both supervised and unsupervised tasks. Our analysis indicates that the model's success is due to its ability to effectively handle out-of-vocabulary words, the trigram's ability to avoid paraphrasing, and the ease with which it can be combined with other models. We believe that this enhanced basic model can serve as a solid foundation for various linguistic analyses, such as stylistic classification and fake news detection. All code and models are available for download at github.com/linguafranca/egm.

Reconstructing three-dimensional faces in complex real-world scenarios poses significant difficulties due to frequently missing or occluded facial details, particularly in images depicting large head orientations. This challenging problem is compounded by the extensive variability of head poses, which significantly expands the potential solution space and complicates modeling efforts. To break down this complex task into more manageable components, our approach focuses on modeling both pose and occlusion. In this regard, we introduce an end-to-end framework called SADRNet, which produces a face that varies based on the orientation and another face that remains invariant, then fuses these faces via a self-alignment mechanism informed by occlusion. Exhaustive testing of our proposed technique on the widely used AFLW2000-3D and Florence datasets shows substantial performance enhancements over existing top-ranking methods. Moreover, our approach achieves simple and broad generalization, demonstrating superior results on more challenging datasets such as the recently launched AFW-3D. The code for SADRNet is available at: https://github.com/ghristi/SADRNet.

This paper delves into the underlying causes for the limited success of distant similar learning methods. It appears that current approaches are unable to effectively tackle classification problems at the scale of ImageNet, due to performance being hindered by a significant drop of at least 4%. It is hypothesized that this decline is resultant from the loss of difficult data examples occurring under distant similar learning. To address this issue, the paper introduces a new task called dynamic learning, which places harder examples at the disposal of more capable models. It is demonstrated that this novel framework is effective in absorbing challenging data, thereby expanding the subset of difficult examples available to the standard model by at least 13%. Furthermore, this approach is shown to yield comparable performance to the capable model, with results being validated across multiple classification tasks including ResNet, ReLU based models and on large-scale datasets such as ImageNet. The findings are then utilized to demonstrate the relationship between distant similar learning and the difficulty of data, which is a key aspect in the theory of the framework. In Dynamic Time-Division Duplexing (TDD), individual subframes can be allocated for uplink or downlink transmission based on fluctuating traffic patterns, reducing bandwidth waste and improving system throughput. However, considering interference and the need for periodic re-synchronization, TDD configurations must be updated periodically, introducing a challenge in scheduling optimal models dynamically. To address this challenge, we propose a dynamic scheduling approach based on a 2x2 non-cooperative static game, where base station models act as self-interested players aiming to minimize their own interference and increase their own throughput. We establish the existence of a Nash Equilibrium (NE) and provide an efficient algorithm to track the shifting NE, thereby scheduling optimal models in real-time. Simulations using real traffic data demonstrate a significant improvement in overall throughput and fair capacity distribution. Furthermore, we show that our proposed algorithm is robust and adaptable to varying traffic conditions, complex TDD configurations, and limited buffer sizes. By leveraging our scheduling algorithm's ability to track the NE in real-time, we are able to keep the system close to its optimal performance even in the presence of rapid traffic changes. Our research provides a practical and efficient solution for dynamic TDD scheduling in 5G systems, enabling real-time scheduling in a fair and efficient manner. Moreover, our work enables further exploration in applying static games in 5G base station scheduling and other similar scenarios. Lastly, our algorithm's uniqueness, which is capable of handling changing payoffs, makes it suitable for incorporation in other applications beyond base station scheduling. In these contexts, our algorithm can be referred to as 'Threshold-Driven Algorithm' (TDA). For instance, TDA can be employed in scenarios such as adaptive learning, environment changes, and combined deterministic and stochastic optimization, among others. In this work, we introduce a novel method to train neural networks for derivative estimation using optimization on Hamiltonian dynamics. We demonstrate that neural networks that estimate Hamiltonians can be used to predict derivatives, and our approach surpasses existing methods in derivative estimation tasks. Furthermore, we establish that this method yields a continuous approximation of derivative estimation, taking into account an expansion term that accounts for local dynamics. We also derive a straightforward learning algorithm for this purpose and show that it boils down to a standard stochastic gradient descent in a special case. To validate our approach, we conduct a range of experiments involving intricate systems and straightforward regression tasks, and our findings are consistent across multiple networks architectures. We discover that Hamiltonian Neural Networks exhibit a preference for the Markov property, resulting in a preference for state-based representations over observation-based representations. This is accompanied by a theoretical analysis that provides a mathematical framework for this preference. Finally, we outline a range of future research possibilities, including integrating this method with reinforcement learning and Hamiltonian-based state reconstruction from observations. All the code for this project is available online at https://github.com/ghaleean/hamiltonian-neural-networks.

Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD) involves identifying the appropriate sense of a word with multiple meanings within a particular context.  Advances in deep learning, specifically using BERT, have led to significant gains in WSD accuracy by employing a zero-shot or few-shot learning approach.  However, these successes are largely attributed to the capabilities of deep learning models in leveraging abundant data and labeling information.  In contrast, context-gloss WSD, which utilizes glosses to define word senses, has seen limited improvement from these developments.  Our research introduces a novel strategy, context-gloss enhancement, that incorporates multiple glosses to enrich the context for a target word, enabling a single BERT-based model to handle various word senses.  We demonstrate this approach to be a cost-effective method for modifying the dataset, which in turn leads to a substantial boost in context-gloss WSD performance, averaging a 10% F-score improvement across 5 datasets.  The context-gloss enhancement approach can be integrated into existing few-shot learning methods to further enhance outcomes.  The code is available at https://github.com/zwang93/WSD-CGE.

This paper investigates the feasibility of identifying top quark production via its decay into W bosons and bottom quarks in proton-nucleus collisions at an 100 TeV center-of-mass energy. Given the expected levels of background and considering detector efficiency, we determine the minimum number of proton-nucleus collisions required to detect this process with 10 inverse femtobarns of data. In situations with sufficiently high luminosity, as seen in future projects such as the Future Circular Collider, observing top quark production becomes straightforward. As an example, with a luminosity of $10^{33}$ cm$^{-2}$s$^{-1}$ and a 100 TeV center-of-mass energy, the average number of top quark events exceeds 500 per month. Additionally, we evaluate the reliability of our findings by comparing them with existing studies on top quark production in proton-proton collisions. As expected, due to the increased overlap between the colliding particles, top quark production is more challenging to detect in proton-nucleus collisions than in proton-proton collisions of the same energy. Nonetheless, detecting this process in proton-nucleus collisions opens up new analytical directions, such as studying the gluon distribution within nucleons through measurements of the top quark process on both proton-proton and proton-nucleus collisions. As a starting point for these types of investigations, we establish reference cross-section values for top quark production in proton-proton and proton-nucleus collisions. For proton-proton collisions at 100 TeV, the calculated cross-section is 5.58 $\pm$ 0.13 nanobarns, whereas for proton-nucleus collisions the calculated cross-section is 157 $\pm$ 4 nanobarns. For both collision types, we find that detecting the process is reliable down to 10 inverse femtobarns of data, as required by the paper's initial investigation parameters. As a further analytical tool, we develop a detector acceptance-weighted estimator for calculating cross-section values in data samples. This estimator takes into account the detector's efficiency and acceptance, as well as the properties of the detected particles, and is independent of the production process beyond the detected particles. As a specific example, applying this estimator to a sample of W boson pairs produced at a 100 TeV center-of-mass energy yields a cross-section value of 4.63 $\pm$ 0.11 nanobarns, which is consistent with the calculated value mentioned earlier. Recent studies on the 64Ni nucleus with a low-spin structure have provided significant insights: combining data from four experiments allowed researchers to identify several 0+ and 2+ excited states below 4.5 MeV, and characterize their properties. Using a Monte Carlo shell model, scientists were able to explain the findings and uncover a surprisingly intricate pattern of shapes existing together, where a high-energy prolate 0+ state at 3463 keV, and a collective 2+ state just above it, 286 keV, marked a first in Ni isotopes. This pattern of shapes existing together is particularly notable because it occurs at low spins, and is driven by a strong monopole interaction, counter to previous assumptions that it only dominates at higher spins, and primarily shapes excitations, rather than coexisting with the ground state. This discovery in 64Ni also marks a difference from 60Ni, where shapes exist together but without the collective 2+ state just above, and 62Ni, where the structure is dominated by a collective 0+ state at a lower energy, and a gap exists between the 0+ and 2+ states. Machine learning models often undergo performance assessment through k-fold cross-validation to facilitate model selection and parameter adjustment. Yet, due to the random partitioning inherent in CV, estimated model performance exhibits significant variability. This unpredictability makes effective parameter tuning challenging, as it introduces substantial uncertainty into the choice of parameters. Moreover, our study reveals that the optimal parameters obtained are excessively sensitive to the manner in which the data is divided, often resulting in suboptimal solutions and significant difficulties in achieving reproducibility. In contrast, our research suggests employing the reduced variance j-k fold CV method, which involves conducting multiple independent assessments across K subgroups within the training set J times. The aim is to mitigate performance estimation's intrinsic instability and facilitate effective parameter tuning by prioritizing variance minimization over bias. In line with this principle, our study advocates for a smaller K than typically adopted and instead invests computational resources in increasing the value of J, as demonstrated across diverse NLP tasks including sentiment analysis, part-of-speech tagging and text classification. The resulting models prove highly responsive to variations in the data and covariate shift, as shown to excel in a range of evaluation metrics including the frequency of optimal solutions obtained, model performance, and classification threshold analysis. A novel approach is proposed to create and assess a respiratory motion-corrected, four-dimensional T2-weighted MRI sequence, which is crucial in radiology and radiotherapy treatments guided by MRI. Data acquisition is continuous via a spiral acquisition method with reordering of Cartesian sampling points (rCASPR) that ensures simultaneous reduction of motion artifacts and acquisition time. A precise reconstruction algorithm based on variational nonlinear least squares (VNLS) effectively removes artifacts caused by motion. The evaluation of this method included evaluation of the VNLS algorithm and comparison of image quality with that of free-breathing MRI. No significant difference in image quality was observed between rCASPR and free-breathing MRI. Moreover, rCASPR reduces motion-induced artifacts more efficiently than free-breathing MRI. Additionally, rCASPR allows for the creation of motion-free images from continuous acquisition data via reordering of Cartesian sampling points in the respiratory domain that correlates with end-expiration phases. This results in the creation of high-quality, motion-free 4D MRI from continuous acquisition data without the need for long acquisition times, and makes this method highly suitable for application in radiology and radiotherapy treatments guided by MRI. The rCASPR method has been tested on continuous spiral acquisition data that can be used for 4D MRI with a respiratory cycle of 5 seconds in acquisition time, and this can be achieved on standard MRI scanners. Furthermore, this method has the potential to be employed in other MRI sequences, such as fluid-sensitive MRI, diffusion-weighted MRI, and contrast-agent enhanced MRI, following the proposed spiral and reordering strategies. The rCASPR method has been made publicly available on the internet for the benefit of the scientific community. The challenges faced in developing this method include the complexity of nonlinear reconstruction algorithms, the vast amount of memory required for large-scale respiratory and spatial sampling point matrices, the time consumed by the VNLS algorithm, the limited choice of spiral acquisition trajectories, and the compatibility issues with different MRI scanners. This has been demonstrated in the proposed T2-weighted turbo spin-echo MRI sequence development. Our experiments with multiple datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of P3, showcasing its superior performance relative to the conventional sampling approach. In particular, P3 achieves a top rank in terms of both estimation precision and computational efficiency in paired-permutation settings.
